title: The verse you keep
hook: choose one verse from the juz' to carry for good

segments.voice: Yesterday, your own voice: Ibn Mas'ud reciting, and the Prophet in tears. Your line was beautify it with your voice. Did you say one line out loud, just to yourself? Day two hundred thirty.

Some people keep a note folded in a wallet for years. A line from a letter, a thing a teacher once said. The paper goes soft at the creases. They don't read it every day. They just know it's there, and on the worst days they take it out. One night, Abu Dharr reports, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stood in prayer and recited a single verse, over and over, until dawn. One verse, a whole night. You've now read thirty-seven surahs. Tomorrow this camp closes. Before it does, there's one thing to take with you: not the whole juz', but one verse from it, kept like that folded note. Today: the verse you keep.
screen: `A NOTE FOLDED IN A WALLET.` → `ONE VERSE, A WHOLE NIGHT.` → `ONE VERSE TO TAKE WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Early Muslims learned the Qur'an slowly. An early report says the companions would take ten verses at a time and not move on until they knew them and had lived them. A kept verse works the same way: not a quotation to admire, but a line that does a job in your life. Here are three from the part we've read. From Ash-Sharh, Surah ninety-four, in Pickthall: But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease. Notice two things. The word is with, ma'a, not after, and some readers take that to mean the ease is already inside the hard thing, not only waiting beyond it. And the line is said twice. Commentators noticed that hardship has the definite article, the hardship, while ease does not, so they read it as one hardship and two eases. A report from Ibn Abbas puts it: one hardship will not overcome two eases. From Ad-Duha, Surah ninety-three, words to the Prophet, tradition says, in a dry season when revelation had paused: your Lord has not forsaken you, nor does He hate you. And from Az-Zalzalah, Surah ninety-nine: And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then. Nothing is too small to count. One for the hard day, one for the lonely day, one for the ordinary day. But the verse you keep doesn't have to be any of these. It might be the whisperer that withdraws, or sleep as a sign. The only test is whether you'll take it out when you need it.
screen: `TEN VERSES AT A TIME.` · `WITH HARDSHIP, EASE — SAID TWICE.` · `NOT FORSAKEN.` · `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT OF GOOD.` · then, large: `ONE VERSE, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the verses of these weeks pass through your mind like cards being shuffled. Don't pick the one that sounds most impressive. Wait for the one that pulls at you, the one that seems to know something about your life right now. When it comes, hold it. Say it silently on the in-breath, and let it settle on the out-breath. If you like, imagine folding it small and putting it somewhere safe inside you. The bell holds the time.
The verse you keep. One line from the juz', chosen, written down and carried, the way the Prophet once kept one verse through a whole night. Today's word.
Your line: one verse, kept. Today, write your verse down by hand, on paper, and put it somewhere you'll see it: a wallet, a mirror, a phone case. Day two hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Favorite verses are kept close: written in calligraphy on walls, memorized to recite in hard moments, or repeated in night prayer; some people return to one verse again and again, as the Prophet is reported to have done.

myth: Surah 94 says ease comes after hardship
it says with: ma'a. some read the ease as already inside the hard thing.
the Prophet once repeated a single verse through a whole night
commentators read 94:5–6 as two eases for one hardship
hardship is definite, ease is not; a report from Ibn Abbas says so.

fork.setup: a hard season comes. which verse from the juz' says the ease is already inside it?
fork.reveal: 94:5–6: with hardship, ease, said twice. ma'a means with, not after.

original.note: Arabic: truly, with hardship is ease (94:5–6).

trapdoor: what you thought: pick a favorite quote.
what it means: keep one verse the way early Muslims learned: few at a time, until it's lived.
what a scholar hears: al-'usr is definite and yusr indefinite, so one hardship, two eases (Ibn Abbas); Abu Dharr's night on 5:118 (Nasa'i, Ibn Majah).

Sunan an-Nasa'i 1010; Sunan Ibn Majah 1350 (Abu Dharr: the Prophet repeated one verse, 5:118, until morning)
report attributed to Ibn Mas'ud and others on learning ten verses at a time (al-Tabari, introduction to Tafsir)
report from Ibn Abbas, one hardship will not overcome two eases (in tafsir of 94:5–6)

notes: Please confirm Pickthall's wording of 94:5–6 and 99:7.
The Abu Dharr hadith (Nasa'i 1010, Ibn Majah 1350) cited from memory; confirm numbers and that the verse was 5:118.
The 'ten verses at a time' report is attributed to Ibn Mas'ud / Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami in al-Tabari; confirm attribution.
'One hardship will not overcome two eases' is reported from Ibn Abbas and also attributed to the Prophet in weaker chains; the script attributes it to Ibn Abbas.
